answer_text:
Let \(a_n=\varphi(n)\). Since \(\varphi\) is a bijection of \(\mathbb N\), the sequence \((a_n)\) is a rearrangement of \(1,2,3,\dots\).

We show that the only possible finite limit is \(1\).

---

### 1. \(L\) cannot be less than \(1\)

Suppose \(L<1\). Choose a number \(r\) such that

\[
L<r<1.
\]

Since \(a_n/n\to L\), there exists \(N\) such that for all \(n\ge N\),

\[
\frac{a_n}{n}<r,
\qquad\text{so}\qquad
a_n<rn.
\]

Now fix \(X\ge N\). On the interval \(\{N,N+1,\dots,X\}\), the values

\[
a_N,a_{N+1},\dots,a_X
\]

are all distinct because \(\varphi\) is injective. There are \(X-N+1\) of them.

But for every \(n\) in that interval,

\[
a_n<rn\le rX,
\]

so all these values lie among the positive integers at most \(rX\). Hence

\[
X-N+1\le \lfloor rX\rfloor\le rX.
\]

Since \(r<1\), for sufficiently large \(X\),

\[
X-N+1>rX,
\]

a contradiction. Therefore,

\[
L\ge 1.
\]

---

### 2. \(L\) cannot be greater than \(1\)

Suppose \(L>1\). Then for sufficiently large \(n\),

\[
\frac{a_n}{n}>1,
\qquad\text{so}\qquad
a_n>n.
\]

Thus there exists \(N\) such that for all \(n\ge N\),

\[
\varphi(n)>n.
\]

In particular, no number in the set \(\{1,2,\dots,N\}\) can be \(\varphi(n)\) for some \(n\ge N\), because if \(n\ge N\), then \(\varphi(n)>n\ge N\).

But \(\varphi\) is surjective, so the \(N\) numbers \(1,2,\dots,N\) must appear among the values

\[
\varphi(1),\varphi(2),\dots,\varphi(N-1),
\]

which are only \(N-1\) values. That is impossible. Hence,

\[
L\le 1.
\]

---

Combining the two inequalities gives

\[
L=1.
\]

This value is indeed attainable, for example by the identity bijection \(\varphi(n)=n\), for which

\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\varphi(n)}{n}=1.
\]

Therefore the only possible value of \(L\) is

\[
\boxed{1}.
\]

27B·v4.method: Counting (injectivity on [N,X] into [1,cX]) rules out L<1; surjectivity contradiction rules out L>1; identity gives L=1.
